modules.title: Introduction to Canva and Social Media Graphics
modules.content:
## Why a Small Business Owner Turned to Canva Overnight  

Maria runs a boutique coffee shop in a bustling downtown neighborhood. One morning she notices that her Instagram feed looks stale, while a nearby competitor’s vibrant posts are pulling in a steady stream of new customers. With no design background and a limited marketing budget, Maria wonders: *Can I create eye‑catching graphics myself, or do I need to hire a professional?*  

She discovers Canva—a web‑based design platform that promises “design made simple.” Within minutes she signs up, picks a template, drags in a photo of her latte art, adds a punchy headline, and publishes the post. The next day her engagement spikes, and she realizes that anyone—even a coffee‑shop owner with no design training—can produce polished social‑media graphics.  

Maria’s story illustrates the power of Canva for beginners who need fast, effective visuals for social media. In this chapter you’ll learn exactly what Canva is, why it’s a go‑to tool for social‑media graphics, how to set up a free account, and how to navigate the dashboard. You’ll also see the key differences between Canva Free and Canva Pro, and get a handy reference of the most common social‑media graphic types and their optimal dimensions.

---

## 1. What Is Canva?  

Canva is an **online graphic‑design platform** that lets users create visual content—such as social‑media posts, flyers, presentations, and more—without needing advanced software like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator. It works entirely in a web browser (with optional mobile apps), so you only need an internet connection and a modern browser to start designing.

### Primary Use Cases for Social‑Media Graphics  

| Use Case | How Canva Helps | Typical Output |
|----------|----------------|----------------|
| **Creating brand‑consistent posts** | Access to brand kits, color palettes, and pre‑sized templates | Instagram posts, Facebook ads |
| **Designing promotional banners** | Drag‑and‑drop elements, animated text options | Twitter header, LinkedIn cover |
| **Making story‑style visuals** | Vertical canvas presets, quick‑resize tools | Instagram Stories, Snapchat |
| **Generating video‑snippets** | Simple animation effects, built‑in music tracks | TikTok clips, Reels teaser |
| **Producing event flyers** | Printable PDFs, high‑resolution export | Facebook event image, printable poster |

In short, Canva gives you **ready‑made layouts**, a **library of assets** (photos, icons, fonts), and **intuitive editing tools** that together make it possible to produce professional‑looking graphics in minutes.

---

## 2. Key Features That Make Canva Ideal for Beginners  

Even if you’ve never touched a design program, Canva’s interface is built around a few core concepts that keep the learning curve shallow.

### 2.1 Drag‑and‑Drop Canvas  

- **What it means** – You click an element (text box, image, shape) and move it directly onto the canvas. No separate “layers” panel or complex menus.  
- **Why it matters** – You can see exactly where an object will appear, making spatial decisions intuitive.

### 2.2 Pre‑Sized Templates  

Canva stores **template libraries** for every major social‑media platform. Each template is already set to the correct pixel dimensions, so you never have to guess whether a 1080 × 1080 image fits Instagram.  

- **Examples**: Instagram Post, Facebook Cover, YouTube Thumbnail, Pinterest Pin.  

### 2.3 Built‑In Asset Library  

- **Free photos** – Over a million royalty‑free images.  
- **Icons & illustrations** – Vector graphics that scale without losing quality.  
- **Fonts** – Hundreds of typefaces, with the ability to upload your own (Pro only).  

All assets are searchable by keyword, and you can filter results by “Free” vs. “Premium”.

### 2.4 Simple Text Editing  

- **Text presets** – Pre‑styled headings, subheadings, and body text that you can apply with a click.  
- **Typography controls** – Font size, color, spacing, and alignment are accessible from a single toolbar.  

### 2.5 Collaboration & Cloud Storage  

- **Real‑time collaboration** – Invite teammates to edit the same design simultaneously.  
- **Auto‑save** – Your work is saved to the cloud automatically, so you never lose progress.  

### 2.6 One‑Click Export  

Export options include PNG, JPG, PDF, MP4 (for animated designs), and GIF. You can also share a design via a link or publish directly to certain social platforms (Pro feature).

These features combine to create a **low‑friction environment**: you focus on the creative decisions (what message, which image) while Canva handles the technical details (size, resolution, file format).

---

## 3. Getting Started: Signing Up for a Free Canva Account  

### 3.1 Step‑by‑Step Registration  

1. **Visit** `www.canva.com`.  
2. Click **“Sign up”** in the top‑right corner.  
3. Choose a registration method:  
   - **Email** – Enter your work or personal email address and create a password.  
   - **Google** – Use your Google account for single‑sign‑on (SSO).  
   - **Facebook** – Connect via Facebook if you prefer.  
4. **Confirm** your email (Canva will send a verification link).  
5. **Complete** the onboarding questionnaire (optional). It asks about your design goals (e.g., “I want to create social media posts”) and helps Canva suggest relevant templates.  

After these steps you land on the **Canva dashboard**, the hub from which you will launch all future designs.

### 3.2 Overview of the Dashboard Layout  

| Area | Description |
|------|-------------|
| **Top Navigation Bar** | Contains the main menu (Home, Templates, Projects, Brand Kit, Apps) and a search box for finding assets or templates. |
| **Left Sidebar** | Shows your recent designs, folders, and shared projects. |
| **Main Workspace** | Central area displaying featured templates, “Create a design” button, and suggested design types based on your activity. |
| **Profile Icon** (top‑right) | Access account settings, upgrade options, and help resources. |

#### Quick Tour  

- **Create a design** – Click the bright orange button labeled “Create a design.” A dropdown lets you pick a specific format (e.g., “Instagram Post”) or enter custom dimensions.  
- **Search bar** – Type “summer sale” to pull up relevant templates, images, or icons.  
- **Brand Kit (Free)** – Even on the free plan you can set a primary color palette and upload a logo (limited to one brand kit).  

Spend a few minutes clicking through each area; the layout is intentionally **consistent** across devices, so the same workflow applies whether you’re on a laptop or the Canva mobile app.

---

## 4. Canva Free vs. Canva Pro: What’s the Difference?  

Canva offers a **freemium** model. The **Free** tier gives you everything needed to start designing, while **Canva Pro** unlocks advanced capabilities for growing businesses or power users. Below is a concise side‑by‑side comparison.

| Feature | Canva Free | Canva Pro |
|---------|------------|-----------|
| **Template library** | Full access to thousands of free templates | All Free templates + **Premium** (paid) templates |
| **Asset library** | ~1 million free photos, icons, and illustrations | Unlimited premium assets (stock photos, videos) |
| **Brand Kit** | 1 brand kit (1 logo, 2 colors, 1 font) | Unlimited brand kits, **custom fonts**, color palettes |
| **Magic Resize** | Manual resizing only | **One‑click** resizing to any preset dimensions |
| **Background Remover** | Not available | Instant removal of image backgrounds |
| **Storage** | 5 GB total | 100 GB (or more) |
| **Collaboration** | Unlimited members | Unlimited members + **approval workflows** |
| **Export options** | PNG, JPG, PDF (standard) | PNG, JPG, PDF (print), MP4, GIF, **transparent PNG** |
| **Scheduling** | Not available | Direct posting/scheduling to Facebook, Instagram, etc. |
| **Price** | Free | $12.99 / month (annual) or $16.99 / month (monthly) |

**When to stay on Free**  
- You’re an individual or small team creating occasional posts.  
- You don’t need premium stock images or the background remover.  

**When Pro adds value**  
- You maintain a **consistent brand identity** across dozens of posts.  
- You need **quick resizing** for multiple platforms (e.g., turning one design into Instagram, Facebook, and Twitter versions).  
- You require **transparent PNGs** for logos or overlays.  

For this beginner chapter, we’ll focus on the **Free** plan, ensuring you can accomplish the core tasks without any subscription.

---

## 5. Common Types of Social‑Media Graphics and Their Ideal Dimensions  

Before you start designing, it helps to know the **standard canvas sizes** for each platform. Using the correct dimensions prevents blurry or cropped images when the graphic is uploaded.

| Graphic Type | Platform(s) | Recommended Dimensions (pixels) | Aspect Ratio |
|--------------|------------|----------------------------------|--------------|
| **Square Post** | Instagram Feed, Facebook Feed, LinkedIn | 1080 × 1080 | 1:1 |
| **Portrait Post** | Instagram Feed (vertical), Pinterest Pin | 1080 × 1350 | 4:5 |
| **Landscape Post** | Twitter Feed, Facebook Feed, LinkedIn | 1200 × 628 (Twitter) / 1200 × 630 (Facebook) | ~1.91:1 |
| **Story / Reel** | Instagram Stories, Facebook Stories, Snapchat | 1080 × 1920 | 9:16 |
| **Cover Photo** | Facebook Cover, LinkedIn Cover, YouTube Channel | 820 × 312 (Facebook) / 1584 × 396 (LinkedIn) / 2560 × 1440 (YouTube) | Varies |
| **Thumbnail** | YouTube, Vimeo | 1280 × 720 | 16:9 |
| **Carousel Slide** | Instagram Carousel | 1080 × 1080 (consistent across slides) | 1:1 |
| **Event Flyer** | Facebook Event, Printable PDF | 1200 × 628 (digital) or 8.5 × 11 in (print) | Varies |
| **Quote Graphic** | Instagram, Pinterest | 1080 × 1080 (square) or 1080 × 1350 (portrait) | 1:1 or 4:5 |

> **Tip:** Canva’s template library automatically sets these dimensions for you. When you click “Create a design” and select “Instagram Post,” the canvas opens at 1080 × 1080 pixels—no manual resizing required.

### 5.1 Quick Reference Cheat Sheet  

- **Instagram** – 1080 × 1080 (post), 1080 × 1920 (story)  
- **Facebook** – 1200 × 628 (post), 820 × 312 (cover)  
- **Twitter** – 1200 × 628 (post)  
- **LinkedIn** – 1200 × 627 (post), 1584 × 396 (cover)  
- **Pinterest** – 1000 × 1500 (pin) – but 1080 × 1350 works well too  
- **YouTube** – 1280 × 720 (thumbnail), 2560 × 1440 (channel art)  

Having these numbers at your fingertips ensures you select the right template and avoid the dreaded “Your image is too small” warning.

---

## 6. Hands‑On: Your First Design in Canva (Free)  

Now that you understand what Canva is, its core features, and the dimensions you’ll need, let’s walk through a concrete, step‑by‑step creation of a simple Instagram post for Maria’s coffee shop.

### 6.1 Choose the Right Template  

1. From the dashboard, click **“Create a design.”**  
2. In the dropdown, select **“Instagram Post.”** A blank 1080 × 1080 canvas appears.  

### 6.2 Add a Background Image  

1. Click **“Photos”** in the left sidebar.  
2. Type **“coffee beans”** into the search bar.  
3. Drag a free‑stock photo onto the canvas. It automatically fills the background.  
4. Adjust opacity (optional) by clicking the image, then the **Transparency** icon (a checkerboard) and sliding to 70 % for a subtle overlay effect.  

### 6.3 Insert Text  

1. Click **“Text”** → **“Add a heading.”**  
2. Type **“New Autumn Blend!”**  
3. Use the top toolbar to set the font to **“Montserrat Bold,”** size **48**, color **#FFFFFF** (white).  
4. Position the heading near the top of the canvas using drag‑and‑drop.  

### 6.4 Add a Call‑to‑Action (CTA)  

1. Add a **subheading** with the text **“Visit us for a free tasting today.”**  
2. Change the font to **“Montserrat Regular,”** size **24**, color **#FFD700** (gold).  
3. Align it just below the main heading.  

### 6.5 Insert a Logo  

1. Click **“Uploads”** → **“Upload media.”**  
2. Select Maria’s logo file (PNG with transparent background).  
3. Drag the logo to the bottom‑right corner. Resize by dragging the corners while holding **Shift** (maintains aspect ratio).  

### 6.6 Export the Design  

1. Click **“Share”** → **“Download.”**  
2. Choose **PNG** (high‑quality for Instagram).  
3. Hit **“Download.”** The file saves to your computer, ready for upload.  

Even with this minimal workflow, Maria now has a polished, brand‑aligned Instagram post created in under ten minutes—no design degree required.

---

## 7. Frequently Asked Beginner Questions  

| Question | Simple Answer |
|----------|---------------|
| **Do I need a powerful computer to use Canva?** | No. Canva runs in any modern browser; even a modest laptop or tablet works fine. |
| **Can I use Canva offline?** | The free web version requires an internet connection. The mobile app offers limited offline editing, but you’ll need to sync later. |
| **Is Canva safe for my business data?** | Canva uses SSL encryption and stores files in secure cloud servers. For highly confidential material, consider downloading files locally after design. |
| **Do I need to credit Canva for the free assets?** | No. Free assets are royalty‑free for commercial use, but premium assets (available on Pro) may have specific licensing terms—always check the asset’s details. |
| **Can I collaborate with teammates?** | Yes—anyone with a Canva account can be invited to edit a design. Real‑time collaboration works on the Free plan. |

---

## 8. Quick Checklist: Before You Start Designing  

- [ ] **Sign up** for a Canva free account and verify your email.  
- [ ] **Familiarize** yourself with the dashboard: top bar, left sidebar, and main workspace.  
- [ ] **Identify** which social‑media platform(s) you’ll be designing for and note their recommended dimensions.  
- [ ] **Gather** any brand assets (logo, brand colors, fonts) you’ll need.  
- [ ] **Select** a template that matches the required dimensions.  
- [ ] **Save** your design frequently (Canva auto‑saves, but a manual “Save” click gives peace of mind).  

Having this checklist handy reduces the chance of missing a crucial step and keeps your workflow smooth.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Canva** is an online, drag‑and‑drop design tool that enables beginners to create professional social‑media graphics without advanced software.  
- Its **core features**—pre‑sized templates, built‑in asset library, simple text editing, and cloud‑based collaboration—remove technical barriers for non‑designers.  
- Signing up for a **free account** gives you immediate access to the dashboard, where you can launch designs, search assets, and store projects.  
- **Canva Free** provides everything needed for basic social‑media graphics, while **Canva Pro** adds premium assets, brand kits, Magic Resize, background removal, and more.  
- Knowing the **standard dimensions** for each graphic type (square post, story, cover, etc.) ensures your designs look crisp on every platform.  

Armed with this foundational knowledge, you’re ready to move on to the next chapter: **Understanding Social Media Platform Requirements**, where we’ll explore how each platform’s audience and algorithm influence visual strategy. Happy designing!

modules.title: Understanding Social Media Platform Requirements
modules.content:
## Why Size Matters: The Impact of Getting Dimensions Right  

Imagine Maya, a boutique‑owner who just photographed her newest summer dress. She uploads the picture to Instagram, Facebook, and Pinterest without changing anything. On Instagram the image looks crisp, but on Facebook it’s blurry, and on Pinterest the top part is cut off. Maya’s followers notice the inconsistency, and her engagement drops.  

The root cause isn’t the quality of the photo; it’s the **pixel dimensions** she used. Every social platform has a “sweet spot” for width and height measured in pixels. When a design is larger or smaller than that spot, the platform either **compresses** (making it fuzzy) or **crops** (hiding important content).  

**Why does this matter?**  

- **First impressions**: Users scroll quickly. A sharp, correctly‑sized image captures attention; a distorted one signals low effort.  
- **Algorithmic favor**: Many platforms give a slight boost to posts that meet native specifications because they load faster and keep users on the site longer.  
- **Brand consistency**: Using the same visual proportions across channels reinforces your brand’s visual language.  

In short, matching the exact dimensions is a low‑effort way to make your graphics look professional and perform better.

---

## Platform‑by‑Platform Dimension Cheat Sheet  

Below is a **quick‑reference table** for the most common image and video sizes as of 2024. Sizes are given in **pixels (width × height)**. When a platform offers a range (e.g., “minimum 600 px”), the **recommended** size is listed.  

| Platform | Content Type | Recommended Dimensions | Aspect Ratio* |
|----------|--------------|------------------------|---------------|
| **Instagram** | Square post | 1080 × 1080 | 1:1 |
| | Portrait post (feed) | 1080 × 1350 | 4:5 |
| | Landscape post (feed) | 1080 × 566 | 1.91:1 |
| | Stories / Reels | 1080 × 1920 | 9:16 |
| | IGTV / Video Feed | 1080 × 1920 (vertical) or 1920 × 1080 (horizontal) | 9:16 / 16:9 |
| **Facebook** | Feed image | 1200 × 630 (link preview) or 1080 × 1080 (square) | 1.91:1 / 1:1 |
| | Cover photo | 820 × 312 (desktop) – 640 × 360 (mobile) | ~2.6:1 |
| | Profile picture | 170 × 170 (display) – upload 400 × 400 for best quality | 1:1 |
| | Video post | 1280 × 720 (minimum) – up to 1080 × 1920 | 16:9 (landscape) |
| **Twitter** | Single image tweet | 1200 × 675 | 16:9 |
| | Multi‑image tweet (2‑4 images) | 1200 × 1200 (square) | 1:1 |
| | Header (cover) photo | 1500 × 500 | 3:1 |
| | Profile picture | 400 × 400 (recommended) | 1:1 |
| | Video tweet | 1280 × 720 (minimum) – up to 1920 × 1080 | 16:9 |
| **LinkedIn** | Feed image | 1200 × 627 | 1.91:1 |
| | Company page cover | 1128 × 191 | 5.9:1 |
| | Profile picture | 400 × 400 (minimum) – 768 × 768 (recommended) | 1:1 |
| | Video post | 1280 × 720 (minimum) – 1920 × 1080 | 16:9 |
| **Pinterest** | Pin (standard) | 1000 × 1500 (ideal) – 2:3 ratio | 2:3 |
| | Pin (square) | 1000 × 1000 | 1:1 |
| | Video Pin | 1080 × 1920 (vertical) – 1080 × 1080 (square) | 9:16 / 1:1 |
| | Board cover | 222 × 150 | 1.48:1 |

\*Aspect Ratio = width ÷ height; it tells you the shape of the image independent of its pixel count.

> **Tip:** If you design at a higher resolution (e.g., 2400 × 2400) and then export at the recommended size, you retain flexibility for future platforms without losing quality.

---

## Beyond the Feed: Profile Pictures, Cover Photos, and Post Images  

Not all graphics serve the same purpose. Understanding the three main categories helps you choose the right canvas in Canva.

| Graphic Type | Primary Use | Typical Size | Design Focus |
|--------------|-------------|--------------|--------------|
| **Profile Picture** | Represents a personal or brand identity; appears next to every post and comment. | Square – 400 × 400 px (minimum) | Keep the focal point centered; avoid text that can be lost at small display sizes. |
| **Cover / Header Photo** | Large banner that appears at the top of a page (Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn). | Wide rectangular – varies per platform (see table) | Use high‑contrast visuals; leave safe zones on the edges because some devices crop differently. |
| **Post Image / Video** | The main content that appears in a feed, story, or pin. | Platform‑specific (see cheat sheet) | Prioritize the visual hierarchy: eye‑catching subject first, then supporting elements. |

### Safe‑zone guidelines  

- **Profile pictures**: Keep essential elements within a central 60 % of the canvas.  
- **Cover photos**: Leave at least 10 % margin on the left/right edges; the center can be wider.  
- **Feed posts**: For vertical images, keep key text or logos at least 100 px from the top and bottom to avoid cropping on mobile.

---

## Canva’s Ready‑Made Templates: Picking the Right Canvas  

Canva’s **template library** includes a “pre‑sized” option for every major platform. Here’s how to make the most of it:

1. **Start a new design** – Click **“Create a design”** on the dashboard.  
2. **Search by platform** – Type “Instagram post”, “Facebook cover”, or “Pinterest pin”. Canva will display the exact pixel dimensions listed above.  
3. **Select a template** – Choose a **ready‑made layout** that already respects the safe‑zone rules. Even if you start from a blank canvas, the dimensions are set correctly from the start.  
4. **Swap assets** – Drag‑and‑drop your own photos, icons, or illustrations from Canva’s **library of assets** onto the template. Because the canvas matches the platform’s requirement, you won’t need to resize or crop later.  
5. **Export** – When you click **“Download”**, select the appropriate file type (PNG for crisp images, MP4 for videos). Canva automatically maintains the canvas size you started with.

> **Pro tip:** For a multi‑platform campaign, duplicate a design and switch the template type (e.g., from “Instagram post” to “Facebook post”). Canva will automatically resize elements, but always double‑check the **safe zones** after conversion.

---

## When the Standard Doesn’t Fit: Custom Dimensions in Canva  

Sometimes you need a size that isn’t listed—think of a **carousel ad on Instagram**, a **YouTube thumbnail**, or a **custom‑size story for a brand‑specific app**. Canva lets you define any width and height:

1. **Custom size entry** – From the home screen, click **“Custom size”** and type the desired pixel dimensions.  
2. **Maintain aspect ratio** – If you want the same shape as a standard post but larger, multiply both width and height by the same factor (e.g., 1080 × 1080 → 2160 × 2160).  
3. **Use guides** – Turn on **“Show rulers & guides”** (under **File > View settings**) to create your own safe zones. Drag guides to the exact pixel positions you need.  
4. **Save as a template** – If you’ll reuse this custom size, click **“Share” → “Template link”** to store it for future projects.  

### Real‑world example  

Jamal runs a local coffee shop and wants a **vertical flyer** for a **QR‑code‑driven loyalty program** that will be printed as a 4 × 6 inches handout. He needs 300 dpi (dots per inch) for print quality:

- Convert inches to pixels: 4 in × 300 dpi = 1200 px; 6 in × 300 dpi = 1800 px.  
- In Canva, set a custom size of **1200 × 1800**.  
- Design the flyer, then export as **PDF Print** for the highest fidelity.

---

## Video Dimensions Across Platforms  

Static images are only part of the story. Short videos (reels, stories, ads) follow similar size rules, but they also have **frame‑rate** and **duration** limits.

| Platform | Recommended Video Size | Max Length | Frame Rate |
|----------|------------------------|------------|------------|
| Instagram Reels / Stories | 1080 × 1920 (vertical) | 60 seconds (Reels) / 15 seconds (Stories) | 30 fps |
| Facebook Feed Video | 1280 × 720 (minimum) – up to 1080 × 1920 | 240 minutes (max) | 30 fps |
| Twitter Video | 1280 × 720 (minimum) – up to 1920 × 1080 | 2 minutes 20 seconds | 30 fps |
| LinkedIn Native Video | 1280 × 720 (minimum) – up to 1920 × 1080 | 10 minutes | 30 fps |
| Pinterest Video Pin | 1080 × 1920 (vertical) or 1080 × 1080 (square) | 15 minutes | 30 fps |

When you create a video in Canva:

1. **Choose “Video”** from the **Create a design** menu.  
2. **Select a pre‑sized template** (e.g., “Instagram Reel”).  
3. **Add animation** – Use Canva’s **basic animation** tools to set entry/exit effects; keep them under 2 seconds to avoid wasting viewer attention.  
4. **Export** – Click **Download**, choose **MP4**, and verify that the **resolution** matches the platform’s recommendation.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Mini‑Workflow  

1. **Identify the platform(s)** you’ll publish on.  
2. **Pick the matching template** in Canva (or set a custom size).  
3. **Insert your assets**—photos, icons, text—making sure the focal point sits inside the safe zone.  
4. **Preview** using Canva’s **“Resize”** tool to see how the design looks on other platforms.  
5. **Export** in the correct file type and resolution.  
6. **Upload** to the social channel; double‑check the preview before you hit “Post”.

Following this workflow eliminates the guesswork that caused Maya’s blurry Instagram post.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Correct dimensions prevent distortion**: Platforms automatically compress or crop images that don’t match their native sizes.  
- **Standard sizes**: Keep a cheat sheet handy for Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, and Pinterest—both for images and videos.  
- **Graphic types differ**: Profile pictures, cover photos, and feed posts each have unique size and safe‑zone requirements.  
- **Canva’s pre‑sized templates** give you the exact canvas you need, letting you focus on design rather than pixel math.  
- **Custom dimensions** are simple to set in Canva; use them for non‑standard ads, print assets, or unique app formats.  
- **Video follows similar rules**: Match resolution, aspect ratio, and length limits to each platform’s specifications.  

By mastering these dimension fundamentals, you’ll create social media graphics that look crisp, load quickly, and reinforce your brand’s professionalism across every channel.

modules.title: Creating Your First Social Media Graphic in Canva
modules.content:
## Getting Started: Your First Canva Project  

Imagine you run a boutique coffee shop and want to announce a “Buy One, Get One Free” weekend on Instagram. You have a great offer, but no design experience. With Canva’s **low‑friction environment** you can turn that idea into a polished graphic in minutes.  

1. **Log in** – Visit Canva (or open the app) and sign in with your Email or Google account.  
2. **Create a new design** – Click the bright **“Create design”** button on the dashboard. A menu of preset sizes appears; choose **Instagram Post (1080 × 1080 px)**. This opens a fresh canvas sized perfectly for the platform you’ll be posting to.  

You now have a blank workspace ready for the next step: picking a template.

## Choosing the Right Template  

Canva’s **template libraries** hold thousands of ready‑made layouts designed for specific social‑media purposes. Because you’re creating a promotional post, look under the **“Social Media”** category or type “sale” in the search bar.  

- **Filter by style** – Use the dropdowns to narrow results by vibe (minimalist, bold, vintage).  
- **Preview** – Hover over a thumbnail to see a larger preview; click to apply it to your canvas.  

When you select a template, Canva automatically populates the canvas with placeholder text, images, and shapes. This is your starting point; you’ll soon replace or adjust each element.

## Understanding the Canva Workspace  

Familiarity with the workspace speeds up every edit.  

| Area | What It Holds | Key Actions |
|------|---------------|-------------|
| **Left panel** | **Template libraries**, **Photos**, **Elements** (shapes, icons, illustrations), **Text** presets | Drag items onto the canvas |
| **Top bar** | **Undo/Redo**, **Zoom**, **File name**, **Share** | Save, duplicate, or access settings |
| **Canvas** | The actual design area where you see your graphic | Click‑and‑drag to move, resize, rotate |
| **Right panel** (appears after selecting an element) | **Properties** such as color, opacity, position, and layer order | Fine‑tune individual items |

The term **“drag‑drop editor”** simply means you click an asset, hold the mouse button, move it where you want, and release. All changes happen in real time, and **auto‑save** records each step to Canva’s cloud storage.

## Adding, Deleting, and Rearranging Elements  

### Adding Elements  

1. **Text** – Click **“Text”** in the left panel, then drag a **Heading**, **Subheading**, or **Body text** onto the canvas.  
2. **Images** – Choose **“Photos”** or upload your own product shot via the **“Uploads”** tab. Drag the image onto the placeholder you want to replace.  
3. **Shapes** – Under **“Elements”**, select a shape (circle, rectangle, line) and drop it onto the design.  

### Deleting Elements  

- Select the element (a blue outline appears) and press **Delete** or click the trash‑can icon that shows up above the canvas.  

### Rearranging Elements  

- **Layer order** matters when items overlap. With an element selected, use **“Position → Forward”** or **“Backward”** in the top bar, or right‑click and choose **“Bring to front”** / **“Send to back.”**  
- **Drag** any element to a new spot; alignment guides (thin pink lines) appear automatically, helping you snap objects into clean rows or columns.  

**Real‑world example:** Replace the template’s placeholder coffee cup image with a photo of your best‑selling latte. Delete the default text (“Your Text Here”) and type “Weekend BOGO Latte!” in its place. Move the new image slightly left so the headline sits nicely beside it.

## Customizing the Layout with Drag‑Drop  

Now that the basic pieces are in place, shape the visual hierarchy:

- **Resize** – Click an element’s corners and drag outward or inward. Hold **Shift** to maintain proportions.  
- **Rotate** – Hover just outside a corner until the rotate cursor appears; drag to spin the element.  
- **Duplicate** – Select an item and press **Ctrl/Cmd + D**. Duplicate copies are useful for repeating icons or background patterns.  
- **Group** – Select multiple items (hold **Shift** while clicking), then click **“Group”** in the top bar. Grouping lets you move or resize them as a single block.  

You can also quickly change colors using the **color picker** that appears in the right panel. Because you’re building a brand‑consistent post, pull the exact brand hue from your brand guide (refer back to the earlier chapter on brand consistency if needed) and apply it to shapes or text.

## Fine‑Tuning Your Design  

Even a simple post benefits from a little polish:

- **Spacing** – Use the **“Spacing”** control (under the top bar when text is selected) to adjust line height and letter spacing, ensuring readability on mobile screens.  
- **Alignment** – Select multiple elements and click **“Align”** (left, center, right) to create balanced rows.  
- **Opacity & Effects** – Lower an image’s opacity to 70 % if you want text to stand out, or add a subtle shadow for depth.  

All these adjustments are made instantly; you can always **undo** with the arrow in the top bar if something looks off.

## Exporting Your Graphic  

When the design feels complete, you need to deliver it in the right file format for Instagram:

| Format | Best Use | Typical Settings |
|--------|----------|------------------|
| **PNG** | High‑quality images, transparent backgrounds | 1 × size (1080 px), “Transparent background” if needed |
| **JPG** | Faster loading, good for photos | 80 % quality recommended for social media |
| **PDF** | Print‑ready or multi‑page documents (not typical for social posts) | “Standard” or “Print” PDF |

**Export steps**

1. Click **“Share”** → **“Download”** in the top right.  
2. Choose **PNG** (recommended for crisp graphics).  
3. Tick **“Transparent background”** only if you need a non‑rectangular shape; otherwise leave it unchecked.  
4. Press **“Download”** – the file saves to your device, ready for upload.

## Saving and Managing Your Design  

Even after you download, keep the original in Canva:

- **Auto‑save** means every change is stored in your account’s cloud storage.  
- To rename the file, click the default name at the top (e.g., “Untitled Design”) and type a descriptive title like **“IG_BOGO_Latte_2024-08-18.”**  
- Organize projects by creating **folders** (e.g., “Instagram Promotions”) and dragging the design into the appropriate folder. This makes future edits or repurposing effortless.  

If you ever need to retrieve the design, simply open Canva, navigate to the folder, and click the thumbnail to resume editing.

## Quick Checklist Before Publishing  

Before you hit “Post” on Instagram, run through this brief audit:

- **Dimensions** – Confirm the canvas size matches the platform (1080 × 1080 px for Instagram feed).  
- **Readability** – Text should be legible on a small phone screen; zoom out to 25 % and check.  
- **Brand Elements** – Logo, brand colors, and font style are present and correctly applied.  
- **File Format** – Exported as PNG (or JPG) with appropriate resolution.  
- **File Naming** – Clear, date‑stamped name for future reference.  

If any item fails, return to the canvas, make the tweak, and re‑export.

## Key Takeaways  

- Opening a new design and selecting the correct **template** gives you a solid foundation for any social‑media graphic.  
- The **drag‑drop editor** lets you add, delete, and rearrange **text, images, and shapes** quickly; use alignment guides and layer controls for tidy layouts.  
- Customization (resize, rotate, duplicate, group) refines the visual hierarchy without needing advanced software.  
- Export in the appropriate **file format**—PNG for crisp graphics, JPG for faster loading—then download or keep the file in Canva’s cloud storage.  
- Naming and organizing designs in folders ensures you can revisit or repurpose your work efficiently.  

By mastering these steps, you’ll be able to produce professional‑looking social‑media graphics from scratch, empowering you to promote offers, events, or any message with confidence.

modules.title: Working with Text and Typography in Canva
modules.content:
## Why Text Can Make or Break Your Social Media Graphic  

Imagine you’re scrolling through Instagram and a post catches your eye—not because of a stunning photograph, but because the **words jump off the screen**. A bold headline, a playful script for a quote, and a clean subtitle all work together to convey the message instantly. In the split‑second world of social media, that visual hierarchy created by typography is often the deciding factor between a scroll‑past and a click‑through.

In this chapter you’ll learn how to **add, style, and arrange text** in Canva so every graphic you create speaks clearly, matches your brand’s voice, and grabs attention.

---

## 1. Adding Text to Your Design  

### 1.1 The Text Button Basics  

1. **Open your design** (or start from a ready‑made layout).  
2. Locate the **“Text”** button on the left‑hand toolbar.  
   * This button opens three pre‑made text presets—**Heading**, **Subheading**, and **Body Text**—plus a **“Add a little bit of text”** option for quick snippets.  
3. Click the preset that matches the amount of copy you need, or choose **“Add a heading”** for a larger, stand‑alone line.  

When the text box appears on the canvas, you can **drag** it to any spot, **resize** it by pulling the corner handles, and **double‑click** to start typing.

### 1.2 Creating Custom Text Boxes  

If you prefer full control:  

1. Click **“Add a little bit of text.”**  
2. A small placeholder box appears.  
3. **Type** your copy, then use the **toolbar that pops up** above the canvas to adjust size, color, and alignment.  

*Tip:* For longer copy (e.g., a promotional flyer), add a **Body Text** box and use the **“Spacing”** controls to increase line height for readability.

---

## 2. Adjusting Font Size, Color, and Alignment  

### 2.1 Font Size  

- **Slider vs. numeric entry:** The toolbar shows a slider for quick changes and a number field for precise sizing.  
- **Responsive design tip:** When designing for multiple platforms, keep the **heading size** at least **24 pt** for mobile readability.  

### 2.2 Font Color  

1. Click the **text color swatch** (usually a black square).  
2. Choose from:  

   * **Default palette** – Canva’s curated colors.  
   * **Document colors** – colors already used elsewhere in your design.  
   * **Brand kit** – if you’ve set up brand colors, they appear here for instant consistency.  

3. For more nuance, click **“+”** to enter a hex code (e.g., `#FF5733`) or use the **gradient** option for a two‑tone effect.  

### 2.3 Alignment  

The **alignment icons** (left, center, right, justified) sit next to the color picker.  

- **Left‑aligned** text works well for body copy and long paragraphs.  
- **Center‑aligned** creates a balanced look for headlines and quotes.  
- **Justified** is rarely used in social media graphics because it can create uneven spacing on narrow screens.  

---

## 3. Building Strong Font Pairings  

### 3.1 What Is a Font Pair?  

A **font pair** combines two typefaces—usually a **display** (decorative) font for headings and a **sans‑serif** or **serif** font for body copy. The goal is contrast **without clashing**, ensuring hierarchy and readability.

### 3.2 Using Canva’s Font Pairing Tool  

1. With a text box selected, click the **“Font”** dropdown.  
2. At the bottom, select **“Font Pairings.”**  
3. Canva suggests pre‑tested combinations. Hover over each pair to see a preview in your design.  

**Pro tip:** Choose a pair that reflects your brand tone:  

| Brand Tone | Recommended Pair | Example Use |
|------------|------------------|-------------|
| Modern & Minimal | *Montserrat* + *Open Sans* | Tech product launch |
| Friendly & Playful | *Pacifico* + *Lato* | Kids’ workshop flyer |
| Elegant & Luxury | *Playfair Display* + *Roboto* | High‑end fashion sale |

### 3.3 Manual Pairing Checklist  

If you prefer to pick fonts yourself, follow this quick checklist:  

1. **Contrast in weight** – Pair a bold heading with a regular‑weight body font.  
2. **Contrast in style** – Combine a serif with a sans‑serif, or a script with a geometric sans.  
3. **Limit to two fonts** – More than two can look chaotic on a small social media canvas.  
4. **Test legibility** – Zoom out to 50 % and ensure the body text remains crisp.  

---

## 4. Adding Text Effects  

### 4.1 Shadows  

1. Select your text box.  
2. Click **“Effects”** in the top toolbar.  
3. Choose **“Shadow.”**  
4. Adjust:  

   * **Offset** – distance of the shadow from the text.  
   * **Direction** – angle of the light source.  
   * **Blur** – softness of the shadow edges.  
   * **Transparency** – opacity of the shadow.  

Shadows can **lift text off a busy background** and improve readability, especially for light‑on‑dark designs.

### 4.2 Outlines (Strokes)  

1. In the **“Effects”** panel, select **“Outline.”**  
2. Set the **thickness** (1–5 px) and **color**.  

Outlines work well for **logo‑style text** or when you need a **high‑contrast effect** without a shadow.

### 4.3 Curved Text  

1. Click the text box, then **“Effects.”**  
2. Choose **“Curve.”**  
3. Drag the **curvature slider** left or right.  

**When to use it:**  

- Circular logos or badge‑style graphics.  
- Emphasizing a short tagline around a central image.  

**Caution:** Curved text can become hard to read if over‑curved; keep the radius gentle for longer phrases.

### 4.4 Additional Effects  

- **Lift:** Adds a subtle 3‑D lift, useful for button‑style calls‑to‑action.  
- **Glitch:** A stylized distortion for tech‑savvy posts (use sparingly).  

All effects are **non‑destructive**—you can toggle them on/off at any time.

---

## 5. Choosing Fonts That Match Your Brand  

### 5.1 Understanding Brand Tone  

Your brand’s **tone of voice** (e.g., professional, playful, sophisticated) should be mirrored in your typography. Ask yourself:  

- Does the brand feel **approachable**? → Choose rounded, humanist fonts like *Nunito* or *Poppins*.  
- Is it **authoritative**? → Opt for strong, geometric fonts like *Helvetica Neue* or *Futura*.  
- Does it convey **luxury**? → Serif or high‑contrast fonts like *Bodoni* or *Didot* work well.  

### 5.2 Using the Brand Kit (If Set Up)  

If you’ve already defined brand colors and fonts in Canva’s **Brand Kit**, they appear automatically in the **font** and **color** dropdowns. This ensures consistency across every post, reinforcing brand recognition.

### 5.3 Quick Font Evaluation Checklist  

| Check | Why It Matters |
|-------|----------------|
| **Readability at small sizes** | Social media feeds are often viewed on phones. |
| **License** | All Canva fonts are free for commercial use, but double‑check if you upload a custom font. |
| **Mood alignment** | The font should evoke the same emotions as your copy. |
| **Compatibility with pair** | Test the heading and body fonts together before finalizing. |

---

## 6. Formatting Text for Readability and Visual Hierarchy  

### 6.1 Hierarchy Basics  

Visual hierarchy guides the viewer’s eye from the most important information to the least. In a typical social media graphic, the order is:  

1. **Headline** – grabs attention.  
2. **Sub‑headline** – adds context.  
3. **Body copy** – provides details or a call‑to‑action.  

Use **size, weight, color, and spacing** to differentiate each level.

### 6.2 Practical Formatting Steps  

1. **Set the headline**:  
   - Font size: 36–48 pt (adjust based on canvas size).  
   - Weight: Bold or extra‑bold.  
   - Color: Brand’s primary color or high‑contrast (e.g., white on dark background).  

2. **Add the sub‑headline**:  
   - Font size: 24–32 pt.  
   - Weight: Medium or regular.  
   - Color: Secondary brand color or a lighter shade of the headline color.  

3. **Insert body copy**:  
   - Font size: 14–18 pt.  
   - Weight: Regular.  
   - Color: Dark gray (`#333333`) for softer contrast than pure black.  

4. **Adjust line spacing (leading)**:  
   - In the toolbar, click **“Spacing.”**  
   - Set **line height** to around **1.2–1.4** times the font size for comfortable reading.  

5. **Add letter spacing (tracking) if needed**:  
   - Slightly increase for all‑caps headings to improve legibility.  

### 6.3 Using Text Boxes vs. Single Text Layer  

- **Separate boxes** give you independent control over each line’s positioning and effects.  
- **One text layer** is useful for short slogans where you want uniform styling.  

**Best practice for social media:** Use **separate boxes** for each hierarchy level. This makes it easier to swap out copy without disturbing the overall layout.

### 6.4 Maintaining Consistency Across Posts  

Create a **text style preset**:  

1. Design a headline the way you want (font, size, color, effects).  
2. With the text box selected, click the **“...”** menu and choose **“Add to brand kit → Styles.”**  
3. Name it “Brand Headline.”  

Now you can apply this style with a single click to any new text box, ensuring uniformity across your campaign.

---

## 7. Real‑World Scenario: Launching a Summer Sale  

Let’s walk through a complete example, applying everything we’ve covered.

### 7.1 Brief  

- **Goal:** Promote a 30 % off summer sale on Instagram Stories (1080 × 1920 px).  
- **Brand tone:** Fun and vibrant, with a youthful audience.  
- **Key copy:**  
  1. **Headline:** “Sun‑shine Savings!”  
  2. **Sub‑headline:** “30 % OFF all swimwear”  
  3. **CTA:** “Swipe up to shop now!”  

### 7.2 Step‑by‑Step  

1. **Start with a template** from the “Story” library that already has a background image of a beach.  
2. **Add a heading**: Click **“Add a heading.”** Type “Sun‑shine Savings!”  
   - Font: *Pacifico* (playful script).  
   - Size: 64 pt, bold.  
   - Color: White (`#FFFFFF`).  
   - Effect: **Shadow** with offset 2 px, blur 4 px, opacity 30 %.  

3. **Add sub‑heading**: Click **“Add a subheading.”** Type “30 % OFF all swimwear”  
   - Font: *Montserrat* (clean sans‑serif).  
   - Size: 36 pt, medium weight.  
   - Color: Brand secondary color `#FFB400`.  
   - Alignment: Center.  

4. **Add CTA**: Click **“Add a little bit of text.”** Type “Swipe up to shop now!”  
   - Font: *Montserrat* (same as sub‑heading).  
   - Size: 24 pt, regular.  
   - Color: White.  
   - Effect: **Outline** 2 px, color `#FF5733`.  

5. **Arrange hierarchy**:  
   - Drag the headline near the top third of the canvas.  
   - Place the sub‑heading directly beneath, leaving ample line spacing (1.3).  
   - Position the CTA at the bottom, using a **curved text** effect to follow the curve of a sun graphic placed in the lower corner.  

6. **Finalize**:  
   - Review on a mobile mockup (Canva’s “Preview” button).  
   - Adjust text size if any line feels cramped.  
   - Export as PNG for Instagram Stories.  

**Result:** A clear visual hierarchy, brand‑aligned fonts, and eye‑catching effects that guide the viewer from headline to call‑to‑action in seconds.

---

## 8. Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | Quick Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----------|
| **Too many fonts** | Over‑enthusiasm for variety. | Stick to **2‑3 fonts** per design. |
| **Unreadable text on busy backgrounds** | Forgetting contrast. | Add **shadow** or **outline**, or place a semi‑transparent overlay behind the text. |
| **Over‑curved text** | Wanting a dramatic effect without checking legibility. | Keep curvature under **15 %** for longer phrases. |
| **Inconsistent sizing across posts** | Manual adjustments each time. | Create **text style presets** in your Brand Kit. |
| **Using script fonts for body copy** | Aesthetic preference over readability. | Reserve script fonts **only for headings or short quotes**. |

---

## 9. Quick Reference Cheat Sheet  

- **Add text:** Toolbar → Text → Choose preset.  
- **Change size:** Slider or numeric box in top toolbar.  
- **Pick color:** Click color swatch → Palette / Hex.  
- **Align:** Left, center, right icons next to color picker.  
- **Font pairing:** Font dropdown → “Font Pairings.”  
- **Effects:** Select text → “Effects” → Shadow / Outline / Curve.  
- **Save style:** Text box → “...” → “Add to brand kit → Styles.”  

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Text hierarchy** (headline → sub‑headline → body) is essential for guiding viewers.  
- Use **Canva’s Text button** to add separate boxes for each hierarchy level, giving you independent control.  
- Adjust **size, color, and alignment** directly from the top toolbar; remember mobile legibility (≥ 24 pt for body).  
- Leverage the **Font Pairing tool** to find balanced combinations that match your brand tone.  
- Apply **effects**—shadow, outline, curve—sparingly to improve readability or add visual flair.  
- Choose fonts that reflect your brand’s personality; use the **Brand Kit** for consistent application.  
- Format with **line spacing, letter spacing, and preset styles** to keep designs clean and repeatable.  
- Guard against common mistakes: limit fonts, maintain contrast, and test readability at actual size.  

With these tools, you can turn plain text into a powerful visual element that captures attention, reinforces your brand, and drives engagement on every social platform. Happy designing!

modules.title: Adding and Editing Images in Your Designs
modules.content:
## Why the Right Image Can Make or Break Your Post  

Imagine you’re preparing an Instagram carousel to announce a new summer‑tote bag. You have a crisp product photo, a vibrant background image, and a few lifestyle shots you captured on your phone. When you drop those pictures into Canva, the difference between a “just‑okay” post and a scroll‑stopping one often hinges on **how** the images are placed, cropped, and enhanced—not just on the text you add. In this chapter you’ll learn to bring any picture—whether it’s yours or a perfect match from Canva’s library—into a design and shape it until it feels tailor‑made for the platform you’re targeting.

---

## Uploading Your Own Photos  

### From Desktop, Mobile, or Cloud  

1. **Desktop upload** – Click the **Uploads** tab in the left‑hand panel, then hit **Upload media**. A file‑explorer window opens; navigate to the folder where your photos live, select one or more files, and click **Open**.  
2. **Mobile upload** – In the Canva app, tap the **+** button, choose **Upload**, then select **Photos** (or **Files**) to pull images from your device’s gallery or file manager.  
3. **Cloud services** – Canva integrates with Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive. From the **Upload media** dropdown, pick the cloud service, sign in if needed, and browse to the image you want.  

> **Pro tip:** If you frequently reuse a set of brand assets (logos, product shots, etc.), create a dedicated folder inside **Uploads**—e.g., “Spring 2026 Product Shots.” This keeps your workspace tidy and speeds up future projects.

### Organizing Uploads in the “Uploads” Folder  

- **Rename files** directly in Canva by clicking the three‑dot menu ► **Rename**. Use clear, descriptive names like *tote‑front‑2026.jpg* rather than *IMG_1234*.  
- **Add tags** (available on paid plans) to group images by theme, season, or campaign.  
- **Delete unused files** regularly; excess assets can clutter the interface and slow down loading.

### Using Your Uploaded Image in a Design  

1. Drag the thumbnail from **Uploads** onto the canvas, or double‑click it to place it automatically in the center.  
2. Resize by pulling the corner handles while holding **Shift** to maintain aspect ratio, or use the **Position** > **Size** fields for exact dimensions.  
3. Layer your image under or over other elements with the **Position** > **Forward/Backward** controls.  

---

## Exploring Canva’s Stock Photo Library  

### Search Tips and Filters  

- **Keywords** – Type specific terms (e.g., “sunset beach”) into the search bar. Canva’s AI suggests related words; click a suggestion to broaden or narrow the pool.  
- **Filters** – After the results appear, use the filter icons to limit by **Orientation** (portrait, landscape), **Color** (dominant hue), or **Style** (illustration, photo).  
- **Safe‑search** – Activate the lock icon to hide potentially sensitive content—useful when designing for family‑friendly brands.

### Understanding Licensing  

- **Free photos** – Marked with a gray “Free” badge; can be used without cost in commercial or personal designs.  
- **Premium (Pro) photos** – Carry a purple “Pro” badge; require a paid Canva subscription or a one‑time credit purchase.  
- **Attribution** – Most Canva stock images are royalty‑free, meaning you do **not** need to credit the photographer. However, always double‑check the license details under the image’s info panel.

### Drag‑and‑Drop Workflow  

1. Locate a photo that fits your concept.  
2. Hover over it; a **+** icon appears—click to add it instantly to the canvas.  
3. If you need the same image in multiple frames (e.g., a carousel), **duplicate** the page (top‑right **Copy page** button) and the image will appear automatically on the new page.

---

## Basic Image Manipulation  

### Cropping  

- **Select** the image, then click **Crop** in the top toolbar.  
- Drag the corners or sides of the overlay to frame the subject you want.  
- Use the **Aspect ratio** dropdown to lock the crop to common sizes (1:1 for Instagram posts, 4:5 for stories, etc.).  
- Click **Done** to apply.

### Resizing and Scaling  

- **Corner handles** let you enlarge or shrink while preserving the original proportions.  
- For precise dimensions, type values into the **W** (width) and **H** (height) fields in the top toolbar.  
- **Lock aspect ratio** (the chain link icon) ensures the image doesn’t distort when you change only one dimension.

### Rotating and Flipping  

- With the image selected, hover near the top‑right corner until a circular arrow appears. Click and drag to rotate freely, or enter a specific angle in the **Rotate** field.  
- For a quick mirror effect, click **Flip** ► **Horizontal** or **Vertical**. This is handy for creating symmetrical layouts or correcting orientation errors.

---

## Enhancing Images with Filters and Adjustments  

### Applying Pre‑Set Filters  

- Click **Edit image** in the top toolbar, then choose **Filters**.  
- Canva offers a palette of named filters (e.g., *Retro*, *Pop*, *Summer*). Hover over each to preview the effect on your photo.  
- Adjust the **Intensity** slider to dial the filter up or down—sometimes a subtle touch is all you need.

### Fine‑Tuning Brightness, Contrast, Saturation, etc.  

1. In the **Edit image** panel, scroll to **Adjust**.  
2. Move the sliders for **Brightness**, **Contrast**, **Saturation**, **Temperature**, **Tint**, and **Sharpness**.  
3. As you slide, the canvas updates in real time, letting you see the impact instantly.  

> **Remember:** Small, incremental changes usually look more natural than aggressive edits.

### Using the “Advanced” Adjustment Panel  

- **Highlights & Shadows** – Control the brightest and darkest parts of the image separately, useful for rescuing under‑exposed photos.  
- **Vibrance** – Boosts color intensity without oversaturating skin tones.  
- **Blur** – Apply a subtle background blur to make foreground text pop, or create a depth‑of‑field effect.

---

## Isolating Subjects with the Background Remover  

### When to Use the Tool  

- **Product shots** where you want a clean, white or colored backdrop.  
- **Portraits** that need to be placed on a patterned background.  
- **Complex collages** where you only need the subject, not the surrounding scenery.

> The Background Remover is available to **Canva Pro** users and those on certain enterprise plans. If you’re on a free account, you can still access a limited number of removals via the **Magic Resize** feature.

### One‑Click Removal Process  

1. Select the image, then click **Edit image** ► **Background Remover**.  
2. Canva’s AI scans the picture and instantly makes the background transparent.  
3. The result appears as a **PNG** with a checkerboard pattern indicating transparency.

### Refining Edges with “Erase” and “Restore”  

- After the automatic removal, a toolbar with **Erase** and **Restore** brushes appears.  
- **Erase** removes any lingering background fragments; adjust brush size for precision.  
- **Restore** brings back accidentally removed parts of the subject—great for fine‑hair or intricate edges.  

### Re‑adding a Background or Using Transparent PNG  

- Drag a new shape (e.g., a solid‑color rectangle) behind the isolated subject to create a custom backdrop.  
- Export the design as a **PNG with transparent background** if you need the isolated element for another project.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Mini‑Project  

### Scenario: Crafting a Promotional Instagram Post for a New Tote Bag  

You’ve just uploaded three product photos: a front view, a side view, and a lifestyle shot of the tote on a beach. You also found a sunny‑sky stock photo that matches the brand’s summer vibe.

#### Step‑by‑Step Workflow  

1. **Create a new Instagram post** using the 1:1 template you saved in Module 3.  
2. **Upload** the three product photos (see “Uploading Your Own Photos”).  
3. **Place the front‑view image** in the center.  
   - Crop it to a square using the **1:1** aspect‑ratio lock.  
   - Apply the **Summer** filter at 30 % intensity to give it a warm glow.  
4. **Remove the background** from the front‑view photo.  
   - Click **Edit image** ► **Background Remover**.  
   - Use **Erase** to clean up any remaining sand on the tote’s edges.  
5. **Add the sunny‑sky stock photo** as a full‑canvas background.  
   - Drag it onto the canvas, send it **Backward** behind the product image.  
   - Reduce its **Opacity** to 40 % so the product stays the focal point.  
6. **Insert the side‑view image** as a smaller thumbnail in the lower‑right corner.  
   - Resize to 25 % of the canvas width, add a subtle **Drop shadow** (Edit image ► **Shadows**) to give depth.  
7. **Add a text overlay** (“New Summer Tote – 20 % Off”) using the typography controls introduced in Chapter 4.  
   - Position the text above the product, set **Contrast** to 120 % for readability against the sky background.  
8. **Export** the final design as a PNG.  
   - Since the background is already part of the design, choose **PNG** for crisp quality on Instagram’s feed.  

By the end of this workflow you’ve **sourced, uploaded, edited, and combined** multiple images—all within a single Canva canvas—producing a polished, platform‑ready graphic.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Issues  

### Image Looks Pixelated  

- **Check the original resolution** – Canva cannot magically increase detail. If the source file is under 800 px on its longest side, consider finding a higher‑resolution version.  
- **Resize with “Fit”** rather than “Stretch” – Keep the image’s aspect ratio; stretching can blur pixels.  

### Photo Doesn’t Fit the Frame  

- Use **Crop** to remove unwanted edges instead of forcing the image to fill the space.  
- Alternatively, add a **border** or **shadow** to the image so the empty area becomes a design element rather than a flaw.  

### Background Remover Not Perfect  

- **Zoom in** (hold **Ctrl** and scroll) to see fine details.  
- Alternate between **Erase** and **Restore** brushes with a small radius (1–2 px) for hair or fur.  
- If the AI struggles (e.g., a very busy background), try a **manual mask**: duplicate the image, apply **Transparency** to the duplicate, and manually draw a shape around the subject.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Upload** your own photos from any device or cloud service, and keep them organized in the **Uploads** panel for quick access.  
- **Search** Canva’s stock library using keywords, filters, and orientation settings; respect licensing differences between free and premium assets.  
- **Crop, resize, rotate, and flip** images using intuitive handles and toolbar fields; always lock the aspect ratio when you need consistent dimensions.  
- **Enhance** pictures with pre‑set filters or manual adjustments (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.) to match your brand’s visual tone.  
- **Background Remover** lets you isolate subjects in a single click; refine edges with the **Erase/Restore** tools for a clean, professional look.  
- Combining these techniques—uploading, editing, and layering—enables you to build compelling social‑media graphics that stand out in crowded feeds.  

Armed with these skills, you’re ready to turn any photo into a high‑impact design that speaks directly to your audience. Happy creating!

modules.title: Using Shapes, Icons, and Illustrations for Visual Appeal
modules.content:
## Why Shapes, Icons, and Illustrations Matter  

When a scrolling user pauses on a social‑media feed, the first thing their eye catches is **visual hierarchy** – the order in which elements draw attention. A well‑placed shape can frame a headline, an icon can replace a word, and an illustration can give personality to an otherwise plain background. In the same way that a headline copy tells *what* you’re saying, shapes, icons, and illustrations tell *how* you’re saying it.  

> **Scenario** – Imagine you’re promoting a “Weekend Flash Sale” for a boutique clothing store. The brand’s colors are already set, and the copy (“50 % OFF – 48 hrs only!”) is ready from the previous chapter on typography. Adding a bold rectangle behind the headline, a shopping‑bag icon next to the offer, and a subtle illustration of confetti will instantly make the post stand out in the crowded Instagram feed.

The tools you need are all built into Canva’s **library of assets** and **intuitive editing tools** you’ve already explored. This chapter walks you through adding and customizing those visual elements, organizing them with grids and frames, creating custom shapes, and using transparency and layering to give your designs depth.

---

## Adding and Customizing Basic Shapes  

### Inserting a Shape  

1. **Open the left‑hand toolbar** and click the **“Elements”** tab.  
2. Under the **“Shapes”** sub‑section, you’ll see basic geometry – rectangles, circles, triangles, and more.  
3. Click the shape you want; it appears on the canvas, centered on your current view.  

> **Tip:** If you can’t see the shape you need, type “rectangle” or “circle” into the search bar at the top of the Elements panel.  

### Resizing, Rotating, and Recoloring  

* **Resizing** – Drag any corner handle outward or inward. Holding **Shift** while you drag maintains the shape’s proportion (perfect for circles).  
* **Rotating** – Hover near a corner handle until the rotate icon (circular arrow) appears, then drag to turn the shape.  
* **Recoloring** – With the shape selected, a color swatch appears in the top toolbar. Click it to open the color picker. Choose a brand color, a preset palette, or enter a HEX code for precision.  

> **Pro tip:** Use the **“Copy style”** button (paint roller) to apply the same color, border, and shadow settings to multiple shapes instantly.  

### Working with Arrows and Lines  

Arrows are just line‑based shapes with a head. To add one:  

1. In **Elements**, search “arrow”.  
2. Choose a straight or curved arrow.  
3. Adjust its length by dragging the ends, and change its direction by rotating.  

**Styling arrows:**  
* **Weight** – Click the arrow, then use the **“Border weight”** slider in the top toolbar to make it thicker or thinner.  
* **End caps** – Some arrow styles let you toggle between solid, open, or double‑ended heads.  

Arrows are handy for directing attention to a call‑to‑action button or highlighting a key statistic.

---

## Exploring Canva’s Icon and Illustration Library  

### Searching Effectively  

Canva’s library contains millions of **icons** (simple, single‑color symbols) and **illustrations** (more detailed, often multi‑color graphics). To find the right asset quickly:  

* Use **keywords** that describe the concept, not the style (e.g., type “shopping bag” instead of “retail”).  
* Add **style filters** – click the “Style” dropdown and select “Flat”, “Line”, “Hand‑drawn”, or “Colored”.  
* For free resources only, toggle the “Free” filter; for premium assets, toggle “Pro”.  

### Inserting and Adjusting Icons  

1. Click the desired icon; it lands on the canvas.  
2. **Resize** with corner handles; **rotate** as needed.  
3. **Recolor** – Icons are vector‑based, so they adopt any color you select in the top toolbar. This makes them perfect for matching brand palettes.  

**Combining icons with text:**  
* Place an icon directly before a keyword (e.g., a calendar icon before “Saturday”).  
* Use **tight line spacing** (found under the “Spacing” button) to keep the icon and text visually cohesive.  

### Combining Icons with Illustrations  

Sometimes a single icon isn’t enough to convey a concept. Pair an icon with a small illustration for added flair:  

* Insert the illustration first, then layer the icon on top.  
* Adjust the **opacity** of the illustration (see the Transparency section) so the icon remains the focal point.  

---

## Grids, Frames, and the Art of Organization  

### Using Grids to Align Elements  

Grids are invisible guides that help you **snap** elements into a clean, balanced layout.  

1. In **Elements**, scroll to the “Grids” category.  
2. Choose a grid layout that matches the number of sections you need (e.g., a 2‑by‑2 grid for four product images).  
3. Drag the grid onto the canvas; it automatically creates placeholder boxes.  

**Filling a grid:**  
* Drag an image or illustration into a grid cell; it snaps and crops to fit.  
* The grid can contain shapes, icons, or text blocks – anything you drop into a cell will be clipped to that cell’s shape.  

### Frames for Shaped Image Crops  

Frames are similar to grids but have a **visible border** (e.g., circles, hearts, or custom shapes).  

1. Search “frame” in the Elements tab.  
2. Select a frame (e.g., a circular frame for a profile picture).  
3. Drag an image into the frame; it automatically conforms to the frame’s shape.  

**Customizing frames:**  
* Change the frame’s **border color** and **thickness** using the top toolbar.  
* Add a **drop shadow** (under “Effects”) to lift the framed image off the background.  

### Highlighting with Overlays  

Overlays are semi‑transparent shapes placed over photos or illustrations to improve text readability.  

* Insert a rectangle, stretch it over the area you want to dim, then lower its **opacity** to 30‑50 %.  
* Change the overlay’s **blend mode** (found under “Transparency”) to “Multiply” for a darker effect without losing color nuance.  

---

## Creating Custom Shapes with the Drawing Tool  

### Accessing the Drawing Tool  

1. Click **“More”** at the bottom of the Elements panel.  
2. Choose **“Draw”** (the pencil‑icon). A small toolbar appears with pen, marker, and brush options.  

### Sketching Your Own Shape  

* **Select a tool** – the “Pen” creates crisp vector lines, while the “Brush” gives a hand‑drawn texture.  
* **Draw** directly on the canvas. Canva records each stroke as a separate line; you can edit points later by clicking **“Edit”**.  

### Turning a Sketch into a Reusable Element  

1. Once satisfied, click **“Done”**.  
2. With the drawing selected, click **“Group”** (Ctrl + G) to lock the strokes together.  
3. To reuse the custom shape in future projects, click **“Add to Favorites”** in the top toolbar. It will appear under the “Favorites” tab in Elements for quick access.  

**Use cases:**  
* Create a branded “speech‑bubble” shape for quotes.  
* Sketch a unique divider line that matches your brand’s hand‑drawn aesthetic.  

---

## Adding Depth with Transparency and Layering  

### Adjusting Opacity  

Opacity (also called **transparency**) controls how see‑through an element is:  

1. Select the element (shape, icon, or illustration).  
2. Click the **checker‑board icon** in the top toolbar.  
3. Slide the bar or type a percentage (e.g., 40 %).  

**Practical tip:** Use a lower opacity for background elements (e.g., a light illustration) and full opacity for foreground calls‑to‑action.  

### Layer Order – Bring Forward / Send Backward  

Canva works on a **stack** of layers. The topmost layer is visible above everything else.  

* **Bring forward** – Moves the selected element one step up.  
* **Bring to front** – Places it at the very top of the stack.  
* **Send backward** – Moves it one step down.  
* **Send to back** – Places it behind all other elements.  

These commands are accessible via the right‑click context menu or the **“Position”** dropdown in the top toolbar.  

### Using Layer Masks (Optional Advanced Technique)  

While not required for beginners, a simple mask can create interesting cut‑outs:  

1. Place a shape (the mask) on top of an image.  
2. Select both, right‑click, and choose **“Mask”**.  
3. The image now conforms to the shape’s outline, giving a clean, custom‑shaped picture.  

---

## Putting It All Together: A Mini‑Project Walkthrough  

### Scenario: Weekend Flash Sale Graphic  

You need a square Instagram post (1080 × 1080 px) that announces a 48‑hour flash sale. The brand colors are teal (#00BFA5) and coral (#FF6F61). The copy is “48 HRS ONLY – 50 % OFF!”  

### Step‑by‑Step Build  

1. **Start with a blank canvas** – select the Instagram Post template from the “Ready‑made layouts” you’ve used before.  
2. **Add a background rectangle**:  
   * Elements → Shapes → rectangle.  
   * Stretch to cover the entire canvas.  
   * Color it teal.  
3. **Insert a semi‑transparent overlay**:  
   * Duplicate the rectangle (Ctrl + D).  
   * Change its color to white, set opacity to 30 %.  
   * Resize to a smaller central area where the text will sit.  
4. **Place the headline** (already styled in the Typography chapter).  
   * Center it inside the overlay.  
5. **Add a shopping‑bag icon**:  
   * Elements → search “shopping bag”.  
   * Choose a flat, single‑color icon.  
   * Color it coral, size it to match the height of the headline, and place it left of the text.  
6. **Insert a confetti illustration**:  
   * Elements → search “confetti”.  
   * Pick a colored illustration, drag it to the top‑right corner.  
   * Reduce opacity to 40 % so it doesn’t overpower the text.  
7. **Create a custom “flash” shape**:  
   * More → Draw → Pen.  
   * Sketch a quick lightning‑bolt shape.  
   * Color it coral, set opacity to 70 %.  
   * Position it behind the headline (right‑click → Send backward).  
8. **Use a grid to showcase product thumbnails**:  
   * Elements → Grids → 2‑by‑2.  
   * Place the grid beneath the overlay, leaving space for the headline.  
   * Drag four product images into the grid cells; they auto‑crop.  
9. **Finalize layering**:  
   * Ensure the headline and icon are on top (bring to front).  
   * Verify the background rectangle is at the back (send to back).  
10. **Preview** – click the “Play” button to see how the elements interact. Adjust any opacity or positioning as needed.  

You now have a balanced, eye‑catching design that uses shapes, icons, illustrations, grids, and transparency to guide the viewer’s eye from the headline to the product images.

---

## Common Pitfalls and Quick Fixes  

| Issue | Why it Happens | Quick Fix |
|-------|----------------|-----------|
| **Icon color doesn’t change** | The icon is a **photo** rather than a vector. | Search again and add the “Flat” or “Line” style icon. |
| **Shape snaps off‑grid** | Snap‑to‑grid is disabled. | Turn on **“Snap to grid”** in the View menu. |
| **Overlay makes text unreadable** | Opacity set too low or color contrast insufficient. | Increase opacity to 40‑50 % or switch overlay to a darker hue. |
| **Custom drawing looks jagged** | Using the “Brush” tool with a low‑resolution canvas. | Switch to the “Pen” tool for clean vector lines, or enlarge the canvas before drawing. |
| **Layer order is confusing** | Too many elements stacked without naming. | Rename layers (click the layer name in the right‑hand “Layers” panel) or group related items. |

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Shapes** (rectangles, circles, arrows) are foundational visual anchors; resize, rotate, and recolor them to fit your brand.  
- **Icons and illustrations** live in Canva’s searchable library; filter by style and color to keep designs consistent.  
- **Grids** align multiple elements, while **frames** give images custom shapes and help highlight focal points.  
- The **drawing tool** lets you craft unique shapes; save them to Favorites for future use.  
- **Transparency** and **layering** create depth—lower opacity for background elements, and control stack order with Bring Forward/Send Backward commands.  

By mastering these visual tools, you can transform a plain social‑media post into a compelling, brand‑aligned graphic that captures attention and drives engagement. Happy designing!

modules.title: Working with Colors and Branding in Canva
modules.content:
## A Brand‑New Instagram Feed in One Hour  
Imagine you’ve just launched a boutique coffee shop and you need to announce the grand opening on Instagram, Facebook, and TikTok. You have a beautiful photo of your storefront, a catchy headline, and a short description. What will make the post *stand out* among the sea of latte‑loving feeds? The secret weapon is **color**—the right hues, the right balance, and the right consistency that instantly signal “this is *our* brand.”  

In the next few pages you’ll learn how to harness color theory, build a custom palette, and apply it across text, shapes, and backgrounds in Canva so every graphic feels unmistakably yours.

---

## 1. Why Color Matters in Social Media Design  

### 1.1 The Psychology Behind Hues  
- **Red** – grabs attention, evokes excitement or urgency.  
- **Blue** – conveys trust, calm, and professionalism.  
- **Yellow** – sparks optimism and friendliness.  

These associations are not rules set in stone, but research shows that viewers form **first‑impression judgments within 0.1 seconds**. A well‑chosen color palette can therefore influence whether a scroll‑stopping user clicks, likes, or moves on.

### 1.2 Consistency Builds Recognition  
When you use the same colors across posts, followers begin to link those tones with your brand. Think of the iconic **Coca‑Cola red** or **Spotify green**; even without a logo, the hue alone triggers brand recall. In the context of the earlier chapters—where we explored template libraries and ready‑made layouts—adding a consistent color scheme turns a generic template into a **brand‑consistent post**.

### 1.3 Platform‑Specific Color Considerations  
Different platforms have varying visual densities. Instagram’s square format thrives on bold, high‑contrast colors, while LinkedIn prefers more muted, professional palettes. Keep the **Understanding Social Media Platform Requirements** in mind as you select your shades.

---

## 2. Foundations of Color Theory  

### 2.1 Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary Colors  
- **Primary**: Red, Blue, Yellow – cannot be created by mixing other colors.  
- **Secondary**: Green, Orange, Purple – each is a 50/50 mix of two primaries.  
- **Tertiary**: Six hues created by mixing a primary with an adjacent secondary (e.g., red‑orange).

### 2.2 The Color Wheel as a Navigation Tool  
Canva’s **Color Wheel** (found under *Elements → Color Palette*) lets you visualize relationships:

| Relationship | How to Build It | Typical Use |
|--------------|----------------|-------------|
| **Complementary** | Colors opposite each other (e.g., blue & orange) | High contrast, eye‑catching CTAs |
| **Analogous** | Colors next to each other (e.g., blue, blue‑green, green) | Harmonious backgrounds |
| **Triadic** | Three colors evenly spaced (e.g., red, yellow, blue) | Balanced yet vibrant schemes |
| **Monochromatic** | Variations in lightness/tint of a single hue | Clean, sophisticated looks |

### 2.3 Warm vs. Cool Colors  
- **Warm** (reds, oranges, yellows) feel energetic and inviting.  
- **Cool** (blues, greens, purples) feel calm and professional.  

When choosing a palette for a coffee shop, you might blend **warm earthy tones** (to evoke roasted beans) with a **cool accent** (like teal) for a modern twist.

---

## 3. Building a Custom Brand Palette in Canva  

### 3.1 Where to Start  
1. **Open a New Design** – any size; the palette will be saved globally.  
2. Click the **+** sign under *Colors* in the top toolbar.  
3. Choose **“Create a new palette.”**

### 3.2 Selecting Your Core Colors  
Follow this practical checklist:

1. **Primary Brand Color** – the hue that will dominate (logo color, storefront sign).  
2. **Secondary Color** – complements or contrasts the primary; used for highlights or calls‑to‑action.  
3. **Accent Color** – a pop that draws attention to important details.  
4. **Neutral Tones** – whites, blacks, grays, or muted versions of your primary for text and backgrounds.  

> **Tip:** Use the **Color Wheel** to test complementary or analogous relationships instantly.

### 3.3 Saving and Naming Your Palette  

- After adding each swatch, click the **pencil icon** to rename it (e.g., “Coffee‑Brown #6B4F31”).  
- When finished, click **“Save palette.”** It now appears in the *Brand Kit* (if you have a Canva Pro account) or under *Your colors* for free users.  

> **Note:** Even without a Pro subscription, the saved palette stays available across all your designs, ensuring brand uniformity.

### 3.4 Exporting Your Palette (Optional)  
If you work with external tools (e.g., Adobe Photoshop), click the **three‑dot menu** next to the palette and select **“Export colors.”** Canva provides HEX codes—a universal format for web and print.

---

## 4. Applying Colors Consistently  

### 4.1 Text  
- **Headlines**: Use the **Primary Brand Color** for maximum impact.  
- **Body Copy**: Opt for a **Neutral Tone** (dark gray) for readability.  
- **Links/CTAs**: Apply the **Accent Color** to stand out.  

**How to change text color:**  
1. Select the text box.  
2. Click the **A** (text color) icon in the top toolbar.  
3. Choose a swatch from *Your colors*.

### 4.2 Shapes & Icons  
- **Background Shapes**: Fill with a **Secondary Color** to create depth without overpowering the main image.  
- **Icons**: Match their fill or stroke to the **Accent Color** for a cohesive look.  

**Quick tip:** Hold **Shift** while selecting multiple shapes, then click the color swatch to apply the hue simultaneously.

### 4.3 Backgrounds  
- For a **solid background**, pick a **Neutral Tone** or a very light tint of your primary color.  
- For a **gradient**, click *Elements → Gradients* and customize the stops using your saved palette.  

### 4.4 Using Canva’s “Brand Kit” (Pro Feature)  
If you have access, the **Brand Kit** lets you lock your palette to the *default* color picker, preventing accidental use of off‑brand colors. Even without it, storing the palette under *Your colors* achieves the same practical outcome.

---

## 5. Matching Exact Brand Colors with Canva’s Color Picker  

### 5.1 When You Have a Specific HEX or RGB Code  
1. Click any color swatch.  
2. In the color dialog, locate the **“#” field** at the bottom.  
3. Paste the HEX code (e.g., **#C69C6D**) and press **Enter**.  

Canva instantly updates the selected element to that exact hue.

### 5.2 Sampling Colors from Images  
Sometimes you need to pull a shade from a photo of your product:

1. Select the element you want to recolor.  
2. Click the **color picker** (the pipette icon) in the color dialog.  
3. Hover over the image and click the desired pixel.  

The sampled color appears as a new swatch—add it to your palette for future use.

### 5.3 Using the “Eyedropper” Across Multiple Designs  
The eyedropper works on any open canvas, even when you’re editing a template from the library. This makes it easy to **match brand colors** when customizing pre‑made layouts introduced earlier.

---

## 6. Fine‑Tuning Colors: Brightness, Contrast, and Saturation  

### 6.1 Understanding the Three Adjustments  

| Adjustment | What It Does | When to Use |
|-----------|--------------|-------------|
| **Brightness** | Lightens or darkens a color uniformly. | Adjust for legibility on different backgrounds. |
| **Contrast** | Increases the difference between light and dark areas. | Make text pop against busy images. |
| **Saturation** | Intensifies or mutes color vividness. | Soften overly bright brand hues for a softer feel. |

### 6.2 Editing an Element’s Color  

1. Select the element (shape, text, or image).  
2. Click **“Adjust”** in the top toolbar (icon looks like sliders).  
3. Move the **Brightness**, **Contrast**, and **Saturation** sliders.  
4. Observe the live preview; Canva auto‑saves your changes.

### 6.3 Practical Example: Turning a Photo‑Based Background into a Brand‑Friendly Canvas  

Suppose you have a high‑resolution photo of coffee beans, but the greens dominate. To align it with your brand’s **warm brown palette**:

1. Apply a **Brown Overlay** (shape with 30 % opacity) using your primary color.  
2. Increase **Contrast** to make the beans stand out.  
3. Reduce **Saturation** slightly to mute the green undertones.  

The result is a background that feels cohesive while still showcasing the product.

### 6.4 Maintaining Accessibility  

High contrast is not only visually striking—it’s essential for accessibility. Aim for a **contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1** between text and background (WCAG AA standard). Canva’s built‑in contrast checker appears when you adjust text color; a small warning icon will pop up if the ratio falls below the threshold.

---

## 7. Workflow: From Palette Creation to Published Post  

Below is a step‑by‑step workflow that ties together everything covered:

| Step | Action | Canva Tool |
|------|--------|------------|
| 1 | Define brand personality (warm, modern, eco‑friendly). | N/A – conceptual |
| 2 | Choose primary, secondary, accent, and neutral colors using the **Color Wheel**. | Color Wheel |
